title: June and the Wobbly Cart
markdown:
The sky wore its grumpiest grey sweater, swirly and cloudy, the sort of sky that usually means a blanket, hot chocolate, and maybe cookies. For June it was a cheerful invitation. She was not an average scout. She did not collect badges for knots or fire, though she was rather good at both. She was a scout of tiny perfect things. She arranged pebbles into circles like miniature moondials. She catalogued fallen leaves by the number of points and the colours of their veins. She could sniff the juiciest wild strawberries from a long way off, even under the biggest greenest leaves. Her camp under the friendly oak was a picture of just-so: compass in a velvet pouch, magnifying glass on a smooth flat stone, a perfectly flattened patch of moss for quiet observation. She liked everything to stay where she had put it.

Today a little wiggly chaos paid a visit. A gust, playful as a puppy after its tail, whooshed through camp. Her prize-winning sparkly pebbles, arranged with such care, went flying. June’s eyebrows hopped toward her hairline. Hands found her cheeks. Heat. The tummy did cartwheels that were not the gymnastics kind.

“Oh, bother and double bother.” She bent to scoop the treasures into a neat pile. The wind, still giggling, nudged a few more away, as if to say catch me if you can. It was not fair. She liked orderly, predictable, neat.

Then a peculiar sound. Not thunder. Not a sleepy cat. A shaky, clanky, oh-dear-I’m-going-somewhere-I-don’t-want-to-go rumble. She peeked through leafy branches, past her now-dishevelled pebbles, and her eyes widened.

Across the bubbling creek a bridge cart was rolling the wrong way. One sturdy wooden wheel had popped off. The rickety rest wobbled like jelly on a trampoline, teetering, tilting, heading for the shimmering water. The bridge it was meant to cross had decided on an early nap: a messy pile of splintery wood and forgotten plans.

Not a job for neat pebbles or catalogued leaves. A job for June the scout.

She scrambled to the bank, heart drumming. “Hello? Is anyone out there? Can anyone hear me?” No answer. Only the creek’s cheerful gurgle and the unhappy creak-creak-creak of the teetering cart.

Kiki. Kiki the koala mechanic, best friend, a brilliant whiz with anything that whirred, clanked, or sputtered. Soft fur that smelled of motor oil and fresh eucalyptus. Paws gentle, strong, and surprisingly nimble.

June raced through the woods, scout boots thump-thump-thump on damp leaf-earth. She found the workshop under the broad fronds of a giant fern. Tools of all shapes lay about with artistic scatter. A half-finished mix of springs, cogs, and gleaming metal steamed gently. Kiki sat on a small wooden stool, oversized goggles on her nose, peering at a tiny stubborn screw.

“Kiki.” June skidded, autumn leaves swirling. “The bridge cart. It’s going to fall right into the creek.”

Kiki looked up, sleepy eyes widening. She set the screwdriver down. “Oh dear. Quite wobbly. But this blasted gizmo is being extra stubborn. Mrs. Higgins’s brand-new self-stirring teapot keeps trying to stir itself off the table. Quite the pickle.” A puff of steam escaped the spout. “I’ll be a little while longer, June-bug. Could you keep an eye on that cart? Just keep an eye?”

June’s shoulders slumped a tiny bit. First pinch: Kiki could not come at once. She was on her own, and the cart crept closer to the watery edge. Fluster mixed with a pricklier worry. How could a small scout stop a big clumsy thing from tumbling in?

She hurried back. The cart now balanced on the very brink, groaning and wobbling. Mr. Nibbles the squirrel scurried past, cheeks bulging with nuts, carrying a long sturdy branch for his winter hoard. What a perfect branch it looked.

June remembered Kiki showing how a simple pulley made heavy things feel almost light, and how the longer the rope, the less you had to pull. A lever. The idea did not click like a pebble into a designated spot. It sprang.

She spotted a sturdy fallen branch nearby, not quite as long as Mr. Nibbles’s, but strong. She needed to push the cart up a little, stop the tilt. If she could get under it—

Mr. Nibbles, startled by her sudden movement, dropped his precious branch. It rolled with a soft thump into the creek and vanished in a swirl. Second pinch. Best lever gone. The cart gave a particularly loud creek, rough wood on muddy bank, damp earthy smell filling June’s nose, and tilted even more. Now or never.

She grabbed her own branch. Thickest end under the wobbly wheel, dug firmly into the bank. Shoulder against the longer end. All her weight.

Heavy. She pushed with all her might. The branch bit deeper. The cart moved: a tiny, almost imperceptible bit, but it moved. The wobbly wheel lifted just enough off the very edge. The stomach-lurching tilt stopped. Stable. For now.

Her heart thumped a happy drum. She had used a lever. Kiki would be proud.

As if summoned, Kiki arrived a little out of breath, trusty wrench in paw. “June? I heard—oh my goodness.” Eyes wide as saucers: precarious cart, makeshift lever, June standing tall. “You used a lever. You figured it out all by yourself.”

Kiki’s mechanic brain whirred. “Quick. Give me a hand pushing here while you pull that end of the branch.” They worked in harmony: June on the long end, Kiki bracing and securing. A final mighty heave, a shared giggle, and the bridge cart sat on solid, if slightly wobbly, ground.

Later, after the cart was tied down super tight with Kiki’s ropes and pulleys, they sat by the creek sharing a crumbly cookie. June looked at her scattered pebbles. The wind, as if sensing a change of heart, had arranged them into a rather pretty swirly pattern. She did not feel flustered. She felt clever, and, dare she admit it, a little happy about the wobbly bits.

Kiki hummed an off-key tune and winked. “Sometimes the best way to fix things is to get a little messy.”

June, the scout who loved order, left the pebbles as the wind had written them. Not a moondial. Still a kind of map: creek, cart, cookie crumbs, and a branch that had been long enough after all. She wiped a smear of creek-mud from her scout badge and, for once, did not mind the smear. Tomorrow she might line the leaves again. Tonight the creek kept talking, and the cart, tied and humble, stayed on the bank where it belonged.
